q.q: Which cell reference means column F, row 12?
q.why: A cell reference gives the column letter first, then the row number. F:12 uses the colon that belongs in ranges.

q.q: How many cells are in the range C3:C9?
q.why: Rows 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8 and 9 are all included, so there are seven cells. Subtracting 9 − 3 = 6 forgets to count the first cell.

q.q: How many cells are in the range A1:C3?
q.why: The range is three columns wide (A, B, C) and three rows deep (1, 2, 3), so 3 × 3 = 9 cells.

q.q: A hockey club keeps Members, Fees and Fixtures on three tabs in one spreadsheet file. What is each tab called?
q.why: Each tab is one worksheet (one grid); the file holding all three is the workbook.

q.q: Text such as 'Surname' at the top of a column, which says what the data means, is called a…
q.why: A label identifies data. A value is a number used in calculations.

q.q: What is the difference between =SUM(A1:A10) and =SUM(A1,A10)?
o: Both add all ten cells, but the second is the older way of writing it
The first adds only A1 and A10; the second adds all ten cells A1 to A10
The first adds all ten cells; the second gives an error because of the comma
The first adds all ten cells A1 to A10; the second adds only A1 and A10
q.why: The colon means 'through to', so A1:A10 is a range of ten cells. The comma lists separate cells, so only A1 and A10 are added – a valid formula, but not a range.

q.q: A cell holds the formula =B2*C2. What do you see when you look at the cell, and where can the formula itself be seen?
o: The cell shows the formula; the result appears in the formula bar
The cell shows the result; the formula appears in the formula bar
The cell shows the result; the formula appears in the sheet's header
The cell shows both the formula and the result side by side
q.why: A cell holding a formula displays the answer. Clicking the cell shows the formula in the formula bar.

q.q: A cell holds 0.25 and is formatted as Percentage. What is shown in the cell?
q.why: Percentage format shows the stored value multiplied by 100, so 0.25 is displayed as 25%.

q.q: Which format keeps the leading zero of the phone number 07700 900456?
q.why: Text stores the characters exactly as typed. As a Number, the leading zero is dropped.

q.q: A column of numbers shows #### instead of values. What is the most likely cause?
o: The formulae in the column contain an error
The numbers have been formatted as Text
The column is too narrow to display the numbers
The cells have been protected by the owner
q.why: #### means the number does not fit; widening the column makes it appear.

q.q: Which feature joins several cells into one and centres a title across them?
q.why: Merge and centre combines the cells into one and centres the text across them. Wrap text keeps a long entry inside one cell over several lines.

q.q: Which feature makes a long heading continue onto a second line inside the same cell?
q.why: Wrap text lets long text continue on a new line within the same cell, so it fits a narrow column.

q.q: A list has 300 rows. Which feature keeps the heading row visible on screen while you scroll down?
q.why: Freeze panes keeps chosen rows visible while scrolling. Print titles repeat a heading row on printed pages, not on screen.

q.q: Which statement about formatting cells is true?
o: Currency format adds a £ to the value used in calculations
It changes how data is displayed but not the value stored
Percentage format changes a stored 0.2 into the number 20
Formatting can only be applied to cells that contain text
q.why: Formatting never changes the stored value: 0.2 shown as 20% still holds 0.2.

q.q: A sports camp sheet records the fee for each child, a sibling discount rate and a parent's phone number. Which formats are most suitable, in that order?
q.why: Money suits Currency, a rate suits Percentage, and a phone number must be Text to keep its leading zero.

q.q: Which character must every formula begin with?
q.why: Every formula and function begins with an equals sign. $ is used for absolute references and * means multiply.

q.q: What does the formula =10+6/2 give?
q.why: Division is done before addition: 6/2 = 3, then 10 + 3 = 13. Getting 8 means the addition was wrongly done first.

q.q: B2 holds 60 and C2 holds 80. What does =(B2+C2)/2 give?
q.why: Brackets are worked out first: 60 + 80 = 140, then 140 ÷ 2 = 70. Without brackets, =B2+C2/2 would give 100.

q.q: Which formula correctly multiplies B4 by C4?
q.why: A formula needs the = at the start and the * operator; x and × are not accepted.

q.q: D2 contains =B2-C2. It is filled down to D3. What does D3 contain?
q.why: Both references are relative, so both move down one row when the formula is replicated.

q.q: A1 holds 14.50 and B1 holds 32. Why is =A1*B1 better than =14.50*32?
o: Numbers typed into a formula cannot be shown as currency
Cell references make the spreadsheet file a lot smaller
Spreadsheets do not allow numbers to be typed in formulae
The answer updates automatically if A1 or B1 is changed
q.why: With cell references the formula always uses the current contents, so the result stays correct when the data changes.

q.q: What is the fill handle?
o: The bar above the grid that shows the formula held in the cell you have selected
The tab at the bottom of the window that switches between worksheets in a workbook
The small square at the bottom right of a selected cell, dragged to replicate a formula
The dollar sign added to a reference so it stays fixed when a formula is copied
q.why: Dragging the fill handle copies a formula into neighbouring cells and adjusts its references.

q.q: A club's budget is in B5 and the amount spent is in C5. Which formula shows the money left?
q.why: Money left is budget minus spent. =C5-B5 is the wrong way round and B5-C5 has no equals sign.

q.q: Which formula finds the lowest value in B2 to B20?
q.why: MIN is the function name and the range needs a colon. =MIN(B2,B20) only looks at the two cells B2 and B20.

q.q: C2:C6 hold 4, a blank cell, 7, the text n/a, and 9. What does =COUNT(C2:C6) return?
q.why: COUNT only counts cells containing numbers: 4, 7 and 9. The blank cell and the text are ignored.

q.q: Which formula counts how many cells in E2:E30 contain the word Paid?
q.why: COUNTIF takes the range first, then a comma, then the condition in double quotation marks.

q.q: B2:B5 hold 10, 20, 30 and 40. What does =AVERAGE(B2:B5) give?
q.why: The total is 100 and there are four numbers, so the mean is 100 ÷ 4 = 25.

q.q: B2:B5 hold 12, a blank cell, 8 and 10. What does =AVERAGE(B2:B5) give?
q.why: AVERAGE ignores blank cells: (12 + 8 + 10) ÷ 3 = 10. Dividing by 4 to get 7.5 wrongly counts the blank.

q.q: D2:D6 hold the quiz scores 18, 25, 20, 31 and 12. What does =COUNTIF(D2:D6,">=20") return?
q.why: 25, 20 and 31 are greater than or equal to 20. Using ">20" would give 2 because it leaves out the score of exactly 20.

q.q: A pupil writes =TOTAL(D2:D7) to add up a column. What is wrong?
o: The range needs a comma instead of a colon
TOTAL is not a spreadsheet function; SUM should be used
A function should not start with an equals sign
The range should be written the other way, D7:D2
q.why: The function that adds a range is SUM. Using =ADD or =TOTAL is a common way to lose marks.

q.q: Why is =SUM(D2:D7) better than =D2+D3+D4+D5+D6+D7?
o: It does not need an equals sign at the start of the formula
It is the only one of the two that will recalculate
It is the only one of the two that will add decimals
It is quicker to write and less likely to contain a mistake
q.why: A function is a ready-made formula, so it is quicker and less error-prone. Both formulae recalculate automatically.

q.q: B2:B4 hold £12.40, £15.00 and £12.20. What does =SUM(B2:B4) display, if the cell is formatted as currency?
q.why: 12.40 + 15.00 + 12.20 = 39.60, shown in currency format as £39.60.

q.q: Which reference stays exactly the same however a formula is copied, down or across?
q.why: $ before both the column letter and the row number locks the whole reference. $F1 and F$1 are mixed references that lock only part of it.

q.q: E2 holds =D2*$H$1 and is filled down. What is in E5?
q.why: D2 is relative so it moves down to D5; $H$1 is absolute so it stays fixed.

q.q: E2 holds =D2*(1-H1) and is filled down. What is in E3?
q.why: Both references are relative, so H1 becomes H2 – probably a blank cell, giving a wrong answer.

q.q: Why should a VAT rate kept in one cell be referenced absolutely in a formula that is filled down?
o: So the rate is shown as a percentage in every row
So the rate cannot be changed by other users
So every copied formula uses that same rate cell
So the rate is included when the sheet is printed
q.why: An absolute reference does not change when the formula is replicated, so every row uses the one VAT rate.

q.q: What usually happens if the $ signs are left out of a reference to a fixed rate cell and the formula is filled down?
o: An error alert appears and the formula cannot be filled down the column
The copied formulae point at blank cells and give wrong answers without warning
The spreadsheet notices the problem and adds the missing $ signs itself
Every copied formula shows #N/A until the $ signs are added to it
q.why: The rate reference moves down with each row onto empty cells, so the answers are silently wrong.

q.q: A taxi firm keeps its price per mile in F1 and each journey's miles in column B. Which formula in C2 can be filled down to work out every fare?
q.why: The miles change on each row, so B2 is relative; the one price per mile must not move, so F1 is absolute.

q.q: A taxi firm's fare formulae all use the price per mile in $F$1. What is the main benefit of keeping the price in one cell?
o: Each journey can have its own price per mile
The price can never be changed by mistake
The price appears in the footer of every page
Changing F1 once makes every fare recalculate
q.why: Every formula refers to F1, so a price change is made in one place and all fares update.

q.q: Which statement describes a relative cell reference?
o: It changes when the formula is replicated, so each row uses its own data
It stays locked when the formula is replicated, so each row uses one cell
It refers to a cell on a different worksheet within the same workbook
It can only be used inside a function such as SUM, MAX or AVERAGE
q.why: A relative reference such as B2 moves with the formula. A locked reference is absolute.

q.q: I2 holds =IF(G2<100,$H$1,$H$2) and is filled down. What does I3 contain?
q.why: G2 is relative so it becomes G3; the two absolute rate cells stay locked.

q.q: Where should a page number go so that it appears on every printed page?
q.why: Footers repeat at the bottom of every printed page, so page numbers keep the pages in order.

q.q: A treasurer wants to print only A1:F20 and not the lookup tables further down. Which feature should be used?
q.why: A print area is a chosen range that is the only part of the sheet printed.

q.q: A table has 14 columns and will not fit across a portrait page. Which setting is most suitable?
q.why: Landscape gives more width, so wide tables with many columns fit better.

q.q: A long member list prints on four pages. Which setting repeats the heading row at the top of every printed page?
q.why: Print titles repeat chosen rows on every printed page. Freeze panes only keeps them visible on screen.

q.q: A pupil needs a printout as evidence of the formulae used, not the answers. Which setting should be chosen?
q.why: Show formulas prints the formulae rather than their results.

q.q: Which best describes a header in a spreadsheet?
o: The first row of the sheet holding column labels
Text repeated at the top of every printed page
The range of cells chosen to be printed
A title merged and centred across row 1
q.why: A header is an area at the top of every printed page, often holding a title or logo.

q.q: A cell turns red automatically when the stock level falls below 5. Which feature is this?
q.why: The format depends on a condition being true, which is conditional formatting.

q.q: Which of these is a range check?
q.why: A range check sets a lower and an upper limit. The others are a list, a type check and a length check.

q.q: Which statement about data validation is true?
o: It proves that any data entered into the cell is correct
It checks that data is sensible, not that it is correct
It colours any cells that contain invalid data in red
It can only be used on cells that hold text, not numbers
q.why: Validation checks input against a rule; a wrong but sensible value is still accepted.

q.q: What does an error alert do?
o: Tells the user which cells contain formulae they cannot edit
Tells the user the data is invalid and asks them to try again
Highlights the cell in red once the data has been accepted
Shows a message when the cell is selected, before any typing
q.why: An error alert appears when data breaks the validation rule. A message on selecting the cell is an input message.

q.q: Which validation check would stop someone typing 'Studnet' instead of Student?
o: A range check of whole numbers from 1 to 16
A list (drop-down) of Adult, Child and Student
A type check that the entry must be a date
A length check of exactly 6 characters long
q.why: A drop-down list only allows the listed entries, so spelling mistakes are prevented.

q.q: A minibus booking cell has the rule 'whole number 1 to 16'. A group really has 8 people but someone types 7. What happens?
o: 7 is rejected and an error alert asks for the correct number
7 is accepted, because validation cannot check that data is correct
7 is accepted but the cell is coloured red as a warning
7 is rejected because it is less than the real group size
q.why: 7 is within the range 1–16, so it is valid. Validation checks data is sensible, not true.

q.q: What is the main advantage of conditional formatting over colouring cells by hand?
o: It stops users from typing invalid data into the cells
It works out the totals for the cells that are coloured
It lets the colours be printed on every page of the sheet
The colours update automatically whenever the data changes
q.why: The rule is checked every time data changes, so no cells are missed or left wrongly coloured. Stopping invalid data is validation.

q.q: A message saying 'Enter a whole number from 1 to 16' appears as soon as a user clicks a cell, before typing. What is this?
q.why: The input message is the optional part of validation shown when the cell is selected. An error alert only appears after invalid data is entered.

q.q: A minibus seats 8. Any group larger than 8 must be shown in red so a second bus is booked. Which rule is correct?
o: Conditional format: cell value greater than or equal to 8 → red fill
Conditional format: cell value greater than 8 → red fill
Conditional format: cell value less than 8 → red fill
Data validation: whole number from 1 to 8 → red fill
q.why: 'Larger than 8' means > 8. Using >= 8 would wrongly colour a group of exactly 8, which fits one bus.

q.q: What is a spreadsheet template?
o: A pre-designed starting point with layout, formats and formulae already set up
A copy of the workbook data kept on another drive in case the file is lost
A recorded sequence of actions that can be replayed with a single click
A validation rule that controls which data can be typed into the cells
q.why: Users add their own data to a template's ready-made layout. The other options describe a backup, a macro and validation.

q.q: Why should the formula cells in a template be protected?
o: To make the formula cells appear on the printout
To make the formulae recalculate more quickly
To stop users accidentally overwriting the formulae
To allow data to be imported into those cells
q.why: Protecting formula cells means users can only type into the input cells, so the tested formulae stay correct.

q.q: Which file type is commonly used to move data from a database into a spreadsheet?
q.why: Comma-separated values files can be read by almost every application. XLTX is a template and XLSM a macro-enabled workbook.

q.q: Which is a benefit of importing data rather than retyping it?
o: The data is checked to be correct
q.why: Imported data is copied exactly as it was in the source. Importing cannot make wrong source data correct.

q.q: What happens when a user opens a template to start a new month's sheet?
o: A new copy is created, so the original template stays unchanged
The template itself is edited, so it must be cleared each month
The template is converted into a CSV file ready for importing
A macro runs to delete the previous month's data from the file
q.why: Opening a template creates a new file, keeping the original ready for next time.

q.q: When importing a text file, the import wizard asks a series of questions. Which is a typical one?
o: Which chart type should be used to display the imported data
Which cells should be protected once the data has been added
Which character separates the fields, such as a comma or a tab
Which macro should be recorded to repeat the import later on
q.why: The wizard asks which file to use, the separator and each column's format.

q.q: Every coach in a club records fees using the same template. Which benefit does this give the treasurer?
o: The sheets share an identical layout, so they are easy to combine
Each coach's figures are guaranteed to be correct before sending
Each coach can choose their own formulae to suit their own team
The sheets no longer need to be saved as they are already stored
q.why: Consistency is a key benefit: identical layouts are easy to compare and combine. A template cannot guarantee the data entered is correct.

q.q: B2 holds 60. What does =IF(B2>60,"High","Low") show?
q.why: 60 is not greater than 60, so the condition is false and the value_if_false is shown.

q.q: C2 holds 3. What does =IF(C2<5,"Reorder","OK") show?
q.why: 3 < 5 is true, so the value_if_true, Reorder, is shown.

q.q: B2 holds 7000. What does =IF(B2>=10000,"Gold",IF(B2>=6000,"Silver","Bronze")) show?
q.why: 7000 is not ≥ 10000, so the second IF is checked: 7000 ≥ 6000, so Silver.

q.q: Which IF function is written correctly?
q.why: The condition comes first, then the true value, then the false value, separated by commas, with text in quotation marks.

q.q: A garden centre uses =IF(B2>=30,0,$E$1) for delivery, where E1 holds £3.50. What is the delivery charge on an order of exactly £30.00?
q.why: 30 >= 30 is true, so the value_if_true, 0, is returned: free delivery.

q.q: Why should a nested IF for Gold (10,000+), Silver (6,000+) and Bronze test >=10000 before >=6000?
o: Otherwise 12,500 steps would meet >=6000 first and wrongly get Silver
Otherwise the formula would need three closing brackets, not two
Otherwise 5,000 steps would meet >=6000 first and wrongly get Silver
Otherwise the spreadsheet would show #N/A for every pupil's result
q.why: An IF stops at the first true condition, so the highest boundary must be tested first.

q.q: How many different results can =IF(B2>=10000,"Gold",IF(B2>=6000,"Silver","Bronze")) give?
q.why: A nested IF with two conditions gives three possible results: Gold, Silver or Bronze.

q.q: In =IF(B2>=30,0,$E$1), why is 0 not in quotation marks?
o: It is the false value; only true values need quotation marks
It is the condition; only the results need quotation marks
It is absolute; only relative values need quotation marks
It is a number; only text results go in quotation marks
q.why: Text results go in double quotes; numbers, cell references and calculations do not.

q.q: Which formula correctly gives Gold for 10,000 steps or more, Silver for 6,000 or more, otherwise Bronze?
q.why: The highest boundary is tested first, text is in quotes and both IFs are closed with two brackets.

q.q: Which column of the lookup table does VLOOKUP search?
o: The column named by the column number
Every column, from left to right
q.why: VLOOKUP always searches down the first column; the column number only says where the answer comes from.

q.q: In =VLOOKUP(A2,$E$2:$G$9,3,FALSE), what does the 3 mean?
o: Search for the lookup value in the third column
Search only the first three rows of the table
Return the answer from the third column of the table
Allow the lookup value to be up to three away
q.why: The column number chooses which column of the table the result comes from.

q.q: =VLOOKUP(B2,$H$2:$J$5,3,FALSE) is used, but the code in B2 is not in the table. What is shown?
q.why: FALSE means exact match only, so a value that is not found gives #N/A.

q.q: Why is the table range in =VLOOKUP(B2,$H$2:$J$5,3,FALSE) written with $ signs?
o: So the table does not move when the formula is replicated
So the prices in the table are shown as currency values
So the table is hidden from users who are typing codes
So VLOOKUP returns an exact match and not the nearest
q.why: Absolute references keep the lookup table fixed. Exact match is set by FALSE, not by the $ signs.

q.q: What does the FALSE at the end of a VLOOKUP mean?
o: The result is shown as TRUE or FALSE
Only an exact match is accepted
The first column is not searched
q.why: FALSE means exact match; if the value is not found the result is #N/A rather than a wrong price.

q.q: A cinema uses =VLOOKUP(B2,$H$2:$J$5,3,FALSE). From which column of the worksheet does the answer come?
q.why: The table runs from H to J; column 1 is H, 2 is I, 3 is J.

q.q: The VLOOKUP table range is written as H2:J5 (no $ signs) and filled down. What is the likely result?
o: The table stays fixed, because VLOOKUP always locks the table range automatically
Every row returns the price from the first row, because the codes are not copied
The table slides down (H3:J6, H4:J7…), so some codes are not found and give #N/A
The formula cannot be filled down, so each row must be typed in again by hand
q.why: Relative references move when replicated, so the table moves too and codes near the top are no longer inside it.

q.q: A cinema stores its ticket prices once in a lookup table used by VLOOKUP. What happens when the Student price in J4 is changed?
o: Only bookings made after the change use the new price
Every booking shows #N/A until the formulae are re-entered
Every booking that uses the Student code updates
Only the first booking that uses the code is updated
q.why: The formulae look the price up each time, so changing it once updates every booking.

q.q: Changing the ticket price in a model to see the effect on profit is called…
q.why: Testing a change to an input and watching the outputs recalculate is what-if analysis.

q.q: Which is a limitation of a spreadsheet model?
o: Its predictions depend on the accuracy of its data and rules
It recalculates the outputs too quickly to compare options
It cannot use formulae to link the inputs to the outputs
Its outputs can never be shown on a chart for a meeting
q.why: A model only predicts; if an estimate such as attendance is wrong, so is the output.

q.q: A school disco charges £8 a ticket. 100 people come, fixed costs are £300 and costs are £2 per person. What is the profit?
A model for a school disco has ticket price, expected attendance and cost per person. Which of these is an output?
q.why: Inputs are the values you change; the profit is worked out by the formulae, so it is an output.

q.q: What is the difference between changing an input and changing a formula in a model?
o: Changing an input changes the model's rules; changing a formula tests a new situation
Changing an input needs a macro; changing a formula needs a template to be opened
Changing an input tests a new situation; changing a formula changes the model's rules
Changing an input is permanent; changing a formula can always be undone afterwards
q.why: Inputs are the values tried in what-if analysis; formulae are the rules of the model itself.

q.q: A disco model predicts a good profit, but on the night it clashes with a big match and few people come. Which limitation does this show?
o: The model recalculated the outputs too slowly
The model's chart used the wrong chart type
The model's inputs were protected from change
Factors not included in the model are ignored
q.why: Things outside the model, such as weather or a clash with another event, are not taken into account.

q.q: Tickets cost £6, 150 people attend, fixed costs are £400 and costs are £1.50 per person. What is the profit?
q.why: Income 6 × 150 = £900; costs 400 + (1.50 × 150) = £625; profit 900 − 625 = £275. £500 forgets the per-person cost.

q.q: Which chart best shows monthly temperatures over a year?
q.why: A line graph shows a trend over time.

q.q: What does the legend on a chart show?
o: The title explaining what the chart is about
The scale and units used on the y-axis
Which colour represents each data series
The exact value shown on each bar or slice
q.why: The legend is the key; the exact values are data labels.

q.q: Month names are in A2:A7 and sales in B2:B7. Which range should be selected to create the chart?
q.why: Select the labels and the data together so the months label the chart.

q.q: Which chart best shows how a £600 budget is divided between five activities?
q.why: A pie chart shows parts of a whole.

q.q: A teacher wants to see whether more hours of revision go with higher test marks. Which chart is best?
q.why: A scatter graph shows the relationship between two sets of numbers.

q.q: A school wants to compare the number of tickets sold for each of its four shows. Which chart is best?
q.why: A column or bar chart compares separate categories. A line graph suggests a trend over time.

q.q: A pupil uses a pie chart to show youth club attendance for each month. What is the best criticism?
o: A pie cannot show more than five slices, so a column chart must be used
A pie cannot be given a title, so readers will not know what it shows
A pie shows parts of a whole; a line graph would show the trend over time
A pie does not update when the data changes, unlike a line graph does
q.why: Data that changes over time suits a line graph; a pie chart is for parts of a whole.

q.q: What is a macro?
o: A ready-made workbook with headings and formulae already set up for others
A small program that stores a sequence of actions so they can be replayed
A rule that changes the look of a cell when a condition is true
A rule that checks data against limits as it is typed into a cell
q.why: A macro automates a repeated task. The other options describe a template, conditional formatting and validation.

q.q: Which file type keeps the macros in an Excel workbook?
q.why: A macro-enabled workbook is saved as .xlsm; otherwise the macro is lost.

q.q: Which task is best suited to a macro?
o: Typing in each new customer's name and address
Deciding what the price of a ticket should be
Clearing the same order form many times a day
Choosing the best chart type for a set of data
q.why: A macro suits a repeated sequence of identical steps.

q.q: A macro was recorded with one wrong step in it. What happens when it is run?
o: It spots the wrong step and leaves it out
It stops and asks the user to fix the step
It repeats the wrong step every time it is run
It refuses to run until it is recorded again
q.why: A macro repeats exactly what was recorded, including mistakes, so it must be tested.

q.q: Why should you only enable macros from sources you trust?
o: Macros from unknown sources always slow the CPU down
Macros from unknown sources delete the template file
Macros from unknown sources can contain malicious code
Macros from unknown sources cannot be saved as .xlsm
q.why: A macro is a program, so an untrusted one could do harm.

q.q: When a macro is recorded in Excel, what is written behind the scenes?
o: A CSV file listing each of the actions
A template file saved with the .xltx type
A validation rule for each cell changed
Code in a scripting language called VBA
q.why: The recorder writes the steps as VBA code, which advanced users can edit.
